comparison: Perfect agreement on dopamine-beta correlation findings (C4, C28-C32). Both evaluations find the evidence SUPPORTED with no methodological concerns. OpenEval emphasizes the quantitative rigor and anatomical specificity (cerebellar control), while peer reviewers explicitly affirm this as a core finding across all three reviewers.

Perfect agreement on GABA control analyses (C33-C38). Both evaluations find the evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval highlights these as important negative controls demonstrating specificity of dopamine-beta relationship. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm the control analyses validate the specificity of dopamine findings and describe this as a strength.

Strong agreement on the main integrative conclusion (C5). Both evaluations find this SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes this is an inference well-supported by convergence of multiple modalities. Peer reviewers affirm this advances circuit-level understanding and creates a unified hypothesis, with all reviewers supporting the integrative nature of the conclusion.

Strong agreement on beta prevalence and spatial distribution findings (C2, C14-C23). Both evaluations find the evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the rigorous FOOOF parametrization and careful data selection. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm the spatial distribution findings with no concerns raised, noting beta is ubiquitous beyond sensorimotor areas.

Strong agreement on functional and structural connectivity findings (C3, C25-C27). Both evaluations find the evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval highlights the robust methodology using FWE-corrected statistics and convergence of functional/structural findings. Peer reviewers affirm the connectivity mapping without methodological concerns, noting compelling evidence for shared networks.

Partial overlap on methodological aspects (C11-C13, C24). OpenEval R1 addresses these as part of the invasive recording evidence supporting beta prevalence. Peer R5 specifically evaluates the methodology and data sources, affirming the multimodal approach as innovative and a major strength without concerns about epilepsy patient data selection.

Partial overlap on dataset quality (C67-C68). OpenEval R2 mentions these large normative datasets as supporting connectivity findings. Peer R5 evaluates the creative use of publicly available datasets as a methodological strength, affirming data quality without raising concerns.

Disagreement on status quo interpretation (C51). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED as accurately representing established theoretical frameworks from prior literature. Peer reviewers rate this UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 3 finding the discussion too speculative and far-reaching given the static nature of data and lack of behavioral measures.

Disagreement on mood-related beta literature (C62). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED as accurately representing prior clinical research with appropriate citations. Peer reviewers rate this UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 3 identifying a gap in the discussion of beta's role in mood, finding the treatment incomplete relative to available literature.

OpenEval evaluated background claims on beta functional roles (C1, C6-C10, C40-C49) as SUPPORTED literature review claims. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addressed these background claims, though they provide context for the novel findings that peer reviewers did evaluate.

OpenEval evaluated methodological justification claims (C55-C57) as SUPPORTED, representing established knowledge about non-invasive limitations and network mapping advantages. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addressed these methodological background claims.

OpenEval evaluated limitations and speculative interpretations (C63-C66) as UNCERTAIN, noting these are explicitly speculative and require empirical validation. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addressed these limitation claims, though peer R7's concerns about speculation may relate to similar issues.
